advances: An ordinary fixed-sector reduction for the spectral objective and an exact conditional quadrilateral witness under the cap ceiling.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Translate $y$ to zero and apply an invertible linear map whose rows are two of the normals. The three normal evaluations become $x,y,-x-y$ in the new coordinates, up to their ordering. The area factor multiplies both each $q_i$ and each coarea $\ell_i$, since the latter is the area derivative in the same raw normal threshold. It also multiplies $k$, so every $f_i$ is preserved. In these coordinates the cyclic ray endpoints are $(A,0),(0,B),(-t,t),(-a,0),(0,-b),(r,-r)$ with radii $R=(A,B,t,a,b,r)$, and the three chord labels may be ordered as $\ell_1=B+b,\ell_2=A+a,\ell_3=t+r$.

Write $W_s$ for the fixed sector areas and $c_s=1/(2W_s)$, with indices modulo six. The prescribed-sector theorem 7d1ee06fa4119930 says that the feasible radii have $R_sR_{s+1}\le2W_s$ and the matrix
$$
L_{ss}=c_{s-1}+c_s-R_s^{-2},\qquad
L_{s,s+1}=L_{s+1,s}=c_s-(R_sR_{s+1})^{-1}
$$
positive semidefinite, with other off-diagonals zero. A core sector has equality in the product bound. The positive diagonal lower bounds on each radius and the product upper bounds give compactness as in 82a8acc237f57498. Thus $J$ attains a maximum at actual data.

At a positive $f$, the largest eigenvalue is simple with a positive unit eigenvector $w$. Taking absolute values improves any mixed-sign Rayleigh maximizer, and a zero of a nonnegative maximizing vector propagates by the eigenvector equation. Hence all maximizing eigenvectors have strict sign, which prevents multiplicity. The simple eigenvalue and its derivatives are smooth locally. If a single inverse chord $x_i=1/\ell_i$ varies, the parameter $\theta=q_i x_i/M$ is a smooth strictly monotone coordinate. In this coordinate $f_i$ is a positive multiple of $\theta$ and the other $f$ entries are positive multiples of $1-\theta$. Write the resulting matrix near the original parameter as $B_0+\epsilon D$. All three edge slopes of $D$ are nonzero, so $\det D\ne0$. At a stationary parameter, $w^\mathsf{T}Dw=0$ and $z=Dw$ is a nonzero vector perpendicular to $w$. The Rayleigh quotient of $w+\epsilon c z$ at $B_0+\epsilon D$, minus its old largest eigenvalue $J$, has numerator
$$
\epsilon^2\bigl(2c\lVert z\rVert^2+c^2 z^\mathsf{T}(B_0-JI)z\bigr)
+\epsilon^3c^2 z^\mathsf{T}Dz
$$
and denominator $1+\epsilon^2 c^2\lVert z\rVert^2$. For small fixed $c>0$ the quadratic coefficient is positive. Thus both sufficiently small nonzero signs of a stationary one-coordinate change increase $J$. Also, degree-zero homogeneity in the chord lengths gives $\sum_i\ell_i d_i=0$ for $d_i=\partial J/\partial\ell_i$.

We now check the feasible moves at a maximum. Increasing a radius with both incident products strict increases the changed entries of $L$ and keeps off-diagonals nonpositive. Such an increase preserves positive semidefiniteness, by comparing the quadratic forms on coordinatewise absolute values. Every endpoint of a positive-derivative chord must therefore touch a core. When all derivatives vanish, every endpoint must touch a core by the strict stationary gain, which needs at least three cores. Otherwise homogeneity gives a positive chord derivative, requiring at least two distinct cores at its opposite endpoints. If $L$ were positive definite, a small decrease of any radius would remain feasible, contradicting a negative derivative or the strict stationary gain. Thus a singular block exists.

In any positive definite connected block an internal radius can vary in both directions, with the other blocks unchanged. This would increase $J$ in one direction, or in both at stationarity. Hence no positive definite block can contain an internal node. With exactly two cores there are two blocks. Relabel the positive-derivative chord as $\ell_1$, at radii $B,b$. Its required cores are one of $(0,3),(0,4),(1,3),(1,4)$. Pairs $(0,3),(1,4)$ make two blocks of size three, so both are singular. For pair $(0,4)$ the only possible positive definite block is the short block on $A,r$. If it were positive definite, we could decrease $A$ by a factor $e^{-s}$ and increase $B$ by $e^s$, or decrease $r$ by $e^{-s}$ and increase $b$ by $e^s$. Each exchange fixes the intervening core product. The increased radius only increases entries of the other block, and positive definiteness of the shortened block persists for small $s>0$. The two first-order conditions would give $Ad_2\ge Bd_1>0$ and $rd_3\ge bd_1>0$, contradicting homogeneity. For pair $(1,3)$ the short block is on $t,a$, and exchanges decreasing $t$ while increasing $B$, or decreasing $a$ while increasing $b$, give $td_3\ge Bd_1>0$ and $ad_2\ge bd_1>0$. This gives the same contradiction.

With at least three cores, suppose there is only one singular block. Its complement is positive definite, and the singular block has at most four nodes. Cyclic relabeling in the following cases preserves the opposite-pair chord convention.
- At a singular singleton $s$, separate decreases at $s+2,s+3,s+4$ leave it unchanged and preserve the positive definite complement. They force all three distinct chord derivatives to be positive, contradicting homogeneity.
- For a singular block on nodes $1,2$, decreases at $4,5$ force $d_1,d_3>0$, hence $d_2<0$. The core-preserving exchange decreasing $A$ and increasing $B$ has derivative $Bd_1-Ad_2>0$. It preserves the complement and increases the affected entries of the singular block.
- For a singular block on $0,1,2$, increasing its internal radius $B$ forces $d_1<0$, while decreasing $b$ in the complement forces $d_1>0$.
- For a singular block on $0,1,2,3$, increases of its internal radii $B,t$ force $d_1,d_3<0$, hence $d_2>0$. Increase $A,a$ by $e^s$ and decrease $r,b$ by $e^{-s}$. The separating core products remain fixed, and the product $br$ decreases in the positive definite complement. The singular block entries increase, and the derivative is $(A+a)d_2-rd_3-bd_1>0$.

Every case contradicts maximality, giving at least two singular blocks. They have independent kernel vectors, so the rank is at most four. The sparse prescribed-sector reconstruction cc5768d4e9bc27ab applies at this maximizing datum because there is a core. It realizes the exact rays and sector areas with at most $\operatorname{rank}L$ vertices. All three chord lengths and cap areas of the maximizing datum are preserved, as is $J$.

Finally, $\det B>0$ and $\operatorname{tr}B=0$ give one positive and two negative eigenvalues. Hence $J>1$ is equivalent to $\det(I-B)<0$, or $\sum_i f_i^2+f_1f_2f_3>4$. Under the cap ceiling the strict triangle incidence theorem b08bdaf82b84ef41 applies to a triangular maximizer. The exact strict triangle cubic bound 33488d4938a6ee4a rules out $J>1$ there, leaving a quadrilateral.
statement: Let $K$ be a planar convex body with interior mark $y$ and spanning normals $v_1,v_2,v_3$ with $v_1+v_2+v_3=0$. Let $q_i$ be the areas of the caps $v_i\cdot(x-y)\ge0$, let $\ell_i$ be their chord lengths divided by $\lVert v_i\rVert$, and let $k=|K|$. Put $M=\sum_i q_i/\ell_i$ and $f_i=2\sqrt{kq_i}/(\ell_iM)$. Let $B(f)$ be the symmetric three-by-three matrix with zero diagonal and cyclic off-diagonal entries $f_i/2$, and write $J=\lambda_{\max}(B(f))$. Over ordinary convex bodies with these same lines, mark and six positive sector areas, $J$ attains its maximum. Every maximizing ray datum has at least two core sectors and at least two singular connected blocks in the prescribed-sector matrix. Thus some triangle or quadrilateral with these same sector areas attains the maximum. If $J>1$ and $q_i/k\le128/279$ for all $i$ on the original body, there is a quadrilateral with the same areas and $J>1$.
title: Quadrilateral reduction for the ordinary planar spectral cubic
